tier_reason: The benchmark code is public (bench/main.cpp with the yybench harness in bench/util/benchmark.cpp). The result page names GCC 13.3.0 and the AMD Ryzen 7 7840H, and bench/makefile at commit 933930c (the last commit touching that result file, 2025-12-20) gives g++ -O3 -std=c++20 -march=native. The page times xjb64 against ulfjack's Ryu, the algorithm behind std::to_chars, so tier A holds.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: GCC 13.3.0 (result file, last touched by commit 933930c on 2025-12-20). At that commit, bench/makefile builds with g++ -O3 -std=c++20 -march=native main.cpp util/yybench/src/yybench.cpp, without -DNDEBUG. The HEAD makefile uses -O3 -std=c++20 -march=native -DNDEBUG for g++, icpx -no-ftz and clang++.
corrections.caveats: First-party benchmark run by the author; no peer review. The README's license line says MIT, but the LICENSE file, the GitHub sidebar and the src/ftoa.cpp header are Apache-2.0, so the license is recorded as Apache-2.0. The bench/ directory vendors third-party code (schubfach, ryu, dragonbox, fmt, yy, zmij, teju, uscale, jnum) under their own licenses; the library sources do not need it. std::to_chars is not benchmarked. Ryu (ulfjack d2s_buffered_n) stands in for it and prints its own exponent format (1.1E-6), so output formats differ across rows; the harness comment in bench/util/benchmark.cpp itself calls the comparison 'somewhat unfair' for this reason. Cycles are yybench tick counts scaled by cycles per tick, best of several runs, with each converter called through a function-pointer table, so only ratios are meaningful. In the newer result files (GCC 15.2.0 and Clang 21.1.6 on the 7840H, Apple clang 17 on M1), the xjb64_comp, yyjson and jnum rows sit at the null-function level in every dataset (about 8 cycles on x86, 3.0 on M1). bench/xjb/xjb_i.hpp and bench/yy/yy_i.hpp compile xjb64_comp and yyjson to a 'return buf' stub when USE_xjb_comp or use_yyjson is 0 (the yy header says it is set to 0 to cut compile time), so those rows did no work in those runs. jnum has no such stub, and its near-null value is unexplained. The cited xjb64 and ryu rows are unaffected, and the GCC 13.3.0 file (last updated 2025-12-20) has real values in every row. Results differ by compiler. With Clang 21.1.6 on the same CPU, xjb64 is 71.1 vs ryu 132.5 cycles (about 1.9x); with GCC 15.2.0 it is 55.7 vs 144.4 (about 2.6x) (derived from page data). The HTML result files predate later algorithm updates. The README's current charts (v1.5.0, 2026-04-13; icpx 2025.0.4 on the 7840H, Apple clang 21 on M1/M5) are SVGs only. PR #22 (2026-07-25, 'Fix buffer overflow') raised src/ftoa.cpp's documented output-buffer requirement from 33 to 34 bytes after a one-byte overrun for negative doubles with 16 integer digits in XJB_NO_MEMMOVE mode. Per the PR's file view, it also added a missing NEON store in to_ascii16 and debug-only bounds checks. Callers that sized buffers to the old 33-byte figure must update. The fix touched src/, not the bench copy that produced the cited numbers, and per the PR file view it does not change the release x86 conversion work, so the numbers are not treated as measured on code later fixed for a hot-path bug.

notes: Every cited number matches the GCC 13.3.0 and Apple M1 result pages (xjb64 60.47 vs ryu 142.53, dragonbox_full 105.79, fmt_full 132.20; random length 62.91 vs 199.36; M1 31.4 vs ryu 98.7), and the metadata checks out (Apache-2.0, 46 stars, last commit 2026-08-10, not archived). Two caveat fixes: the run predates -DNDEBUG in the makefile, and the near-null rows in newer files are compile-time stubs of other libraries, not optimized-away work. Shortcomings to record: std::to_chars not run directly (Ryu stands in, with a different output format); first-party; README says MIT while LICENSE is Apache-2.0; PR #22 raised the documented buffer requirement to 34 bytes after a one-byte overrun.

tier_reason: The benchmark code is public (tests/benchmarks.cpp, Google Benchmark) and the result page names clang 16.0.6 with a release build. But no compiler flags are printed and no CPU model is given (only '16 X 3300 MHZ CPUs'), so it is not A. With first-party numbers only, it is C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Only the virtual_ptr rows beat the baseline. In docs/benchmarks/v010500.euclid.clang.md (clang 16.0.6, release build, 100 hierarchies of 1000 objects, run 2024-04-26), arity 1 with an ordinary base: virtual function 60.1, direct virtual ptr 10.5 (ratio 0.18), indirect virtual ptr 12.2 (0.20). Arity 2 with an ordinary base: virtual function 93.2, direct virtual ptr 19.4 (0.21), indirect 20.5 (0.22). That is about 5x lower time per call (derived from page data); the page gives no time unit. With virtual inheritance, the virtual_ptr rows are about 2.1x slower than the virtual function (arity 1: direct 156.9 vs 74.3; arity 2: 231.9 vs 107.3). Every other open-method row is slower than the virtual function: ratios 1.09-1.62 with an ordinary base and 2.05-2.47 with a virtual base. The Performance section of ORIGINAL-README.md says that dispatching a method with one virtual argument takes 15-30% more time than the equivalent virtual member function, and that virtual_ptr makes dispatch 'even faster - three instructions and two memory reads'.
corrections.hardware: host 'euclid', '16 X 3300 MHZ CPUs' (CPU model not stated; cache sizes printed with implausible units: L1 Data 32768 KiB x2, L2 524288 KiB x2, L3 4194304 KiB x8)
corrections.caveats: Weak evidence of 'faster'. The repo was archived on 2026-03-04 and is superseded by Boost.OpenMethod (Boost 1.90). The current README is a retirement notice saying YOMM2 'was' a library, and the original documentation now lives in ORIGINAL-README.md. The author's own text there says open methods are almost as fast as virtual functions and take 15-30% more time with plain references. The benchmark page shows ratios of 1.09-1.62 for every non-virtual_ptr row with an ordinary base (for example, arity 1: basic policy 80.4 vs virtual function 60.1), and 2.05-2.47 with a virtual base. The 0.18-0.22 ratios for virtual_ptr come from a layout effect in tests/benchmarks.cpp. The virtual_ptr rows copy a fat pointer, which already carries the vtable pointer, out of a contiguous vector (population::vptr_draw / ivptr_draw; the vectors are built during allocation, outside the timed loop). The virtual-function row dereferences a randomly chosen heap object (population::draw returns *objects[dist(rnd)]), so cache misses on the object dominate the baseline. In real code that touches the object, the gap would shrink. With virtual inheritance, virtual_ptr dispatch is about 2.1x slower than the virtual function. The result file gives no time unit, no compiler flags and no CPU model; its cache sizes are printed with implausible units (L1 Data 32768 KiB). The benchmark source excludes g++ ('Don't benchmark g++ until this is fixed', GCC bug 85282). The 'much faster than other implementations' claim in docs/articles/performance.md has no numbers. First-party measurement, so tier C.

notes: The numbers match the page, the metadata checks out (BSL-1.0, 382 stars, last commit 2026-02-01, archived 2026-03-04, so abandoned) and the record's caveats hold up against tests/benchmarks.cpp. The only fix: the 15-30% slower statement is in ORIGINAL-README.md, not README.md. Shortcomings to record: ordinary dispatch is 1.09-2.47x slower than virtual functions; the roughly 5x virtual_ptr win is a benchmark layout effect (a contiguous fat-pointer vector vs randomly drawn heap objects); virtual_ptr is 2.1x slower with virtual inheritance; no CPU model; archived and superseded by Boost.OpenMethod (Boost 1.90, a possible lead). Category: 'polymorphic-dispatch' is not a spec category, and none fits exactly, since the baseline is a language feature rather than a std facility. The closest is wave 1 smart-pointers-and-refcount, which already holds std::function/dispatch replacements (woid, Delegate, inplace_function) and fits virtual_ptr as a fat-pointer type.
